overview: The Chitimacha are a living people of southern Louisiana’s bayous and the Atchafalaya Basin. Their reservation is near Charenton. This narrative also serves the map’s “Chtimacha” label: overlapping outlines dated 1492 to 1500 and 1530 to 1783 are imported coverage phases, not separate nations or the people’s beginning and end.

periods.title: Bayou communities
periods.summary: Waterways connected settlements, seasonal travel and trade across southern Louisiana.

periods.title: War and land pressure
periods.summary: French warfare displaced communities; later generations struggled to retain land.

periods.title: Community institutions and renewal
periods.summary: Families strengthened schools and passed on language and cultural skills.

items.text: Bayou Teche and neighboring waterways were routes for trading and visiting, as well as sources of food. Heritage interpreters describe village buildings made with timber, rivercane and palmetto leaves. People adapted journeys and settlement to changing seasons and water levels, using detailed knowledge of their watery surroundings.

The wetlands offered fish, shellfish and other foods alongside edible plants. Traveling through channels required knowing where water led and how conditions changed. The heritage account describes Chitimacha people sharing knowledge of local food, housing and navigation with Acadian newcomers after their arrival in 1765.

Clans documented in the early twentieth century included wolf, bear, dog and lion. Membership passed through the mother’s line. The Tribe’s historical account also describes differences in social rank and forms of address, showing that manners and family connections helped organize community life.

French slave raids helped provoke a war lasting from 1706 to 1718. French forces and Native allies attacked Chitimacha communities; many people were enslaved. Peace ended the fighting, but survivors had been pushed from eastern settlements toward Grand Lake and Bayou Teche.

Landownership remained contested after Louisiana became part of the United States. Lawsuits, pressured sales and tax judgments reduced the land base. In 1916, remaining tribal land entered federal trust. Chitimacha voters later approved a constitution in 1970, with federal approval following in 1971.

Chitimacha baskets begin with local rivercane, a kind of bamboo. Weavers work with red, black and yellow as well as the cane’s natural color. Earlier dyes came from plants; the Tribe also describes later use of commercial dyes. Careful preparation makes a tough stalk into flexible weaving material.

Basket shapes suit different jobs: trays and sifters help with food preparation, while elbow baskets are used to gather berries. Double-woven baskets with lids store belongings, and some can even hold water. That is an impressive assignment for a container made from strips of a plant.

Ada Thomas learned basketry around age twelve from her grandmother Christine Paul, who taught at the reservation school. Her aunt Pauline Paul continued the teaching. Grades one through eight shared one room, so classroom learning and the passing on of family skills could happen close together.

Thomas prepared cane by selecting, splitting, peeling, curing and drying it. For a double-woven basket she formed the inside first, then turned the strips back to build the outside in a continuous weave. The two surfaces are connected parts of one planned structure, rather than a lining dropped into a finished container.

A lidded basket Thomas made in 1989 is preserved at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Its rivercane sides carry the pattern called Alligator Entrails, while small track-like motifs decorate the lid. Named patterns let the viewer recognize a design vocabulary alongside the precision of the weaving.

After eighth grade, Thomas could attend neither the local white nor the local Black high school. She moved to New Orleans to continue studying. Following years away, she returned to basketmaking in the mid-1970s and became a National Heritage Fellow in 1983. Her achievement grew through both family teaching and personal persistence.

sections.title: Schools, a written sentence and care

items.text: In the early twentieth century, some Chitimacha children were sent far away to Carlisle’s boarding school, where they were forbidden to use their language. At home, exclusion from public schools led the community to hold classes in a tribal member’s house in 1932. Families had to struggle for education on their own terms.

The state supplied a condemned school building in 1934, and tribal members repaired it for their children. It remained in use until a new school opened in 1978 with funding mainly from the Bureau of Indian Affairs. The history of a classroom can also be a history of community labor.

A recorded Chitimacha sentence is “we haksigam hix siksi his nuytiqi,” meaning “the young man answered the eagle.” Linguist Daniel Hieber prints it from Benjamin Paul’s recorded narrative material. This example uses the modern practical spelling of a documented utterance, rather than an invented ancient inscription.

Benjamin Paul and Delphine Decloux Stouff helped preserve Chitimacha through work with linguist Morris Swadesh. Paul died in 1932 and Stouff in 1940, but their documentation later supported language revival in the tribal school and early learning center. Written records and remembered knowledge became resources for new learners.

The contemporary RiverCane elder program combines independent housing with practical support. Its published services include meals, grocery trips, social activities and checks of blood pressure and blood sugar. Meals can also reach people unable to travel. Looking after a community includes the ordinary work of helping neighbors eat, meet and stay well.

ending.text: Neither imported map cutoff marks the end of the Chitimacha. The Tribe continues in Louisiana, and children can learn from language documentation preserved by earlier generations. The older record and later “Chtimacha” label belong to this continuing history.
